extracted.intended_audience: writers, preachers, and students of rhetoric and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing persuasive sermons, essays, and orations that elevate the reader, combine moral instruction with rhetorical force, and follow classical rules for the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence grounded in the power of doctrine/content
rubrics_metrics.description: “I confess I can ascribe this Excellence to nothing but the Power of the Doctrines he delivered.” (on St. Paul) — the highest eloquence arises from the force and truth of what is said rather than mere ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance first: ensure your argument or doctrine has intrinsic moral/intellectual force. Rhetorical skill should amplify real, weighty content rather than substitute for it. Example: St. Paul's effect on hearers is attributed to the doctrines he preached, which made listeners' hearts 'burn within us.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave visible marks/lasting effect on readers/hearers
rubrics_metrics.description: “No one Orator has left us so visible Marks and Footsteps of his Eloquence as our Apostle.” — writing/speaking should produce discernible, lasting influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for rhetoric that endures: memorable images, moral clarity, and demonstrable impact on readers' beliefs or behavior. A work that merely delights in the moment but leaves no trace fails this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style to audience and institutional constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: At Athens St. Paul “confines himself to strict Argument only” because “all Attempts upon the Affections and Strokes of Oratory were expressly forbidden…in Courts of Judicature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match rhetorical techniques to the context. Where emotional appeals are inappropriate or prohibited, rely on strict reasoning. Consider legal, cultural, or genre conventions when choosing tone and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary personal narrative and great themes to achieve the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The Discourse on the Resurrection and the Harangue before Agrippa “are truly Great, and may serve as full Examples to those excellent Rules for the Sublime.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reach the sublime, employ grand themes (conversion, resurrection, universal claims), vivid exempla, and intense moral conviction. Follow classical rules for the Sublime (as Longinus and other critics set out): elevation of thought, force of expression, and emotional intensity grounded in truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine instruction with additional rhetorical excellence (sermons can be improved)
rubrics_metrics.description: “However instructive their Sermons are, they are capable of receiving a great Addition; which St. Paul has given them a noble Example of.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional or didactic prose should not be merely informative; rhetorical techniques (structure, examples, passionate appeals when appropriate) can enlarge its effect. Strengthen sermons/essays with clearer organization, memorable phrasing, and suitable rhetorical ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize works that refine and exalt the rational mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “The finest Works of Invention and Imagination are of very little Weight, when put in the Balance with what refines and exalts the rational Mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge writing by its capacity to elevate thought and moral understanding. Prefer content that cultivates reason and virtue over mere cleverness or fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to present exemplary objects/characters for imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealed religion “sets forth a proper Object for Imitation, in that Being who is the Pattern, as well as the Source, of all spiritual Perfection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing moral or didactic works, provide models (characters, ideals, images) readers can emulate; ensure the representation of virtue is clear and attractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select ideas that raise the mind and inspire noble sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: No. 635: the editor chooses Platonic notions because “they contribute to raise the Mind, and may inspire noble Sentiments of our own future Grandeur and Happiness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subject matter and perspectives that lift readers intellectually and morally. Material that merely titillates or flatters the senses fails this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incoherent, mixed, or inconsistent style
rubrics_metrics.description: “Trust me that book is as ridiculous, Whose incoherent style, like sick men's dreams, Varies all shapes, and mixes all extremes.” (Horace, Ars Poetica paraphrase)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain stylistic coherence: consistent tone, unified diction, and orderly structure. Mixing incompatible styles or shifting registers without purpose undermines credibility and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize genuine sentiment and well-wrought characters over ornate pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the sentiments and manners please, And all the characters are wrought with ease, Your tale, though void of beauty, force, and art, More strongly shall delight, and warm the heart; Than where a lifeless pomp of verse appears, And with sonorous trifles charms our ears.” (Horace, Ars Poetica paraphrase)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional truth and believable characters matter more than flashy or sonorous verbal ornament. If forced ornament undermines feeling, it should be removed in favor of natural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound judgment is the ground of writing well
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sound judgment is the ground of writing well.” (Horace, Ars Poetica paraphrase)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply critical taste and measured choice in matters of structure, diction, and argument. Good judgment governs what to include, what to omit, and how to balance ornament and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine greatness cannot be cheaply imitated
rubrics_metrics.description: “Such all might hope to imitate with ease: Yet while they strive the same success to gain, Should find their labour and their hopes are vain.” (on imitation of great models)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect easy success by mimicking great authors; strive for authentic voice and inward conviction. Imitation without depth yields poor results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diversion and variety to refresh the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mind ought sometimes to be diverted, that it may return the better to thinking.” (Phaedr. Fab.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pacing and variation (episodes, lighter passages, changes of scene or tone) can renew reader attention and make returns to serious argument more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flashy openings that end in smoke; strive for substantive surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: “One with a flash begins, and ends in smoke; Another out of smoke brings glorious light, And (without raising expectation high) Surprises us with dazzling miracles.” (Hor. Ars Poet. ver. 143 paraphrase)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not start with mere fireworks that fail to deliver. Better to build from modest openings to genuinely surprising and substantial developments. Promise and performance must align.
